notes.definition: Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It has sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes, but it is not pure water in the chemical sense because it still contains some dissolved substances.
explanation: Water of appropriate quality is essential for life. For humans, drinking water must be potable: it must have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes to be safe. Potable water is not 'pure' in the chemical sense. A pure substance contains only one element or compound, but tap water contains dissolved ions such as calcium, magnesium and chloride ions, as well as small amounts of chlorine added during treatment.

The methods used to produce potable water depend on the available supplies of water and local conditions. In the United Kingdom, rain provides fresh water (water with low levels of dissolved substances). Rainwater collects in the ground (in porous rocks called aquifers), and in lakes, reservoirs and rivers. Most potable water in the UK is produced by choosing an appropriate source of fresh water, passing the water through filter beds to remove solids, and then sterilising it.

Filtration removes insoluble solids such as leaves, twigs, sand and grit. Filter beds of sand and gravel trap smaller particles. Sterilising kills microbes (bacteria and other pathogens) that could cause disease. Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet (UV) light. Chlorine has the advantage that a small amount stays in the water and continues to protect it as it travels through the pipes.

If supplies of fresh water are limited, for example in hot dry countries such as those in the Middle East, desalination of salty water or sea water may be required. Desalination can be done by distillation (boiling the water and condensing the steam, leaving the salts behind) or by processes that use membranes, such as reverse osmosis, where sea water is forced at high pressure through a membrane that lets water molecules through but not dissolved salts. Both methods require large amounts of energy, so desalination is expensive and is used only where fresh water is scarce.

Required practical 8 involves analysing and purifying water samples from different sources. You test the pH of each sample (using universal indicator or a pH meter), and measure the mass of dissolved solids by evaporating a known volume of water to dryness in a weighed evaporating basin and reweighing it. You then purify a sample of salty water by distillation, collecting the distilled water in a cooled test tube or with a Liebig condenser. Pure water has a pH of 7, leaves no residue on evaporation and boils at exactly 100 °C.

keyTerms.definition: Water that is safe to drink, with sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes.
A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.
Water with low levels of dissolved salts, such as rainwater, river water and groundwater.
Porous rock underground that holds water (groundwater).
Killing microbes in water, using chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.
Removing dissolved salts from salty water or sea water, by distillation or by reverse osmosis.
A desalination process in which salty water is forced under high pressure through a membrane that allows water but not salts to pass.
Boiling a solution and condensing the vapour, so the solvent (water) is separated from dissolved solids.

equations.name: Mass of dissolved solids
equations.formula: mass of dissolved solids = mass of basin + residue − mass of empty basin

equations.name: Concentration of dissolved solids
equations.formula: concentration = mass of dissolved solids ÷ volume of water

workedExamples.title: Mass of dissolved solids
workedExamples.question: An empty evaporating basin has a mass of 45.62 g. 50.0 cm³ of river water is evaporated in it. The basin and residue then have a mass of 45.68 g. Calculate the mass of dissolved solids and the concentration in g/dm³.
workedExamples.answer: 0.06 g of dissolved solids; concentration 1.2 g/dm³

workedExamples.title: Comparing water samples
workedExamples.question: Sample A has pH 7 and leaves 0.00 g of residue. Sample B has pH 7.5 and leaves 0.14 g residue from 25 cm³. Sample C has pH 8 and leaves 0.90 g from 25 cm³. Identify which is distilled water and which is most likely sea water.
steps: Pure (distilled) water has pH 7 and leaves no residue: sample A.
Sea water has a high concentration of dissolved salts, so leaves the most residue.
Sample C: 0.90 ÷ 0.025 = 36 g/dm³, typical of sea water.
workedExamples.answer: A is distilled water; C is most likely sea water.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think potable water is pure water.
misconceptions.right: In fact potable water contains dissolved salts and small amounts of chlorine; it is safe to drink but not chemically pure.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think filtration removes dissolved salts and microbes.
misconceptions.right: In fact filter beds remove insoluble solids; microbes are killed by sterilising and dissolved salts need desalination to remove them.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think desalination is used everywhere because the sea is a huge source of water.
misconceptions.right: In fact desalination needs large amounts of energy, so it is expensive and used mainly where fresh water is scarce.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think chlorine is added to make water taste better.
misconceptions.right: In fact chlorine is a sterilising agent added to kill microbes.

realWorld: In the UK, most tap water comes from reservoirs, rivers and aquifers, filtered and then chlorinated.
Countries such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates rely on large desalination plants using reverse osmosis or distillation.
Some swimming pools and water treatment works use ozone or UV light to sterilise water.
examTips: If asked to define potable water, mention both 'safe to drink' and 'low levels of dissolved salts and microbes'.
Learn the UK sequence in order: suitable source, filter beds, sterilise. Name a sterilising agent (chlorine, ozone or UV).
For desalination, always mention that it requires large amounts of energy, which is the main disadvantage.
In the required practical, remember to measure the mass of the empty basin first and to heat gently to avoid spitting.
To show distilled water is pure, give its boiling point (100 °C) or show that it leaves no residue on evaporation.

questions.question: What is potable water?
options: Pure water with nothing dissolved in it
Water that is safe to drink
Water that has been distilled
Water collected directly from rain
markScheme: 1 mark: water that is safe to drink
questions.explanation: Potable means safe to drink. It is not chemically pure, and it does not have to be distilled.

questions.question: Which of these is used to sterilise water in the UK?
options: Sand
Sodium chloride
Chlorine
Carbon dioxide
markScheme: 1 mark: Chlorine
questions.explanation: Chlorine kills microbes. Sand is used in filter beds to remove solids, not to sterilise.

options: To remove insoluble solids
To remove dissolved salts
To kill bacteria
To change the pH to 7
markScheme: 1 mark: to remove insoluble solids
questions.explanation: Filtration removes insoluble particles. Dissolved salts pass through a filter, and microbes are killed by sterilising.

questions.question: Which method could be used to produce potable water from sea water?
options: Filtration
Chlorination
Reverse osmosis
Adding ozone
markScheme: 1 mark: Reverse osmosis
questions.explanation: Sea water must be desalinated. Reverse osmosis uses a membrane to remove salts. Filtration and sterilising do not remove dissolved salts.

questions.question: Why is desalination not the main method of producing potable water in the UK?
options: Sea water contains too many microbes
The UK has plenty of fresh water and desalination requires large amounts of energy
Desalination produces water that is not safe to drink
Desalination only works in hot countries
markScheme: 1 mark: UK has enough fresh water and desalination needs a lot of energy
questions.explanation: Rain supplies plenty of fresh water in the UK, which is much cheaper to treat than sea water.

questions.question: A student tests four water samples. Which result shows that a sample is pure water?
options: pH 7 and a residue left after evaporation
Boils at 102 °C
pH 6 and no residue
Boils at exactly 100 °C and leaves no residue
markScheme: 1 mark: boils at exactly 100 °C and leaves no residue
questions.explanation: Pure water has a fixed boiling point of 100 °C and contains nothing dissolved. Dissolved substances raise the boiling point and leave a residue.

questions.question: In the required practical, why should the evaporating basin be heated gently near the end of evaporation?
options: To stop the solid spitting out of the basin
To make the water boil at 100 °C
To change the pH of the water
To kill microbes in the residue
markScheme: 1 mark: to stop the solid spitting out
questions.explanation: Strong heating makes the solid spit, so some mass is lost and the measured mass of dissolved solids would be too low.

questions.question: A student distils salty water. The thermometer reads 100 °C. Where is the thermometer bulb and why?
options: In the salty water, to measure the boiling point of the solution
In the collecting tube, to check the distillate is cool
At the opening to the condenser, to measure the temperature of the vapour that distils
Inside the condenser, to check the cooling water temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: at the side arm/condenser opening, measuring the vapour that is distilling
questions.explanation: The bulb sits level with the side arm so it reads the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser. 100 °C shows water is distilling.

questions.question: Why is chlorine often preferred to UV light for sterilising water that travels through long pipes?
options: Chlorine removes dissolved salts
Some chlorine remains in the water and continues to kill microbes in the pipes
UV light makes the water toxic
Chlorine is the only sterilising agent that kills bacteria
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine remains in the water and keeps killing microbes
questions.explanation: UV only acts while the water is being treated. Residual chlorine gives ongoing protection in the distribution pipes.

questions.question:
A student evaporated a water sample in an evaporating basin.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the mass of dissolved solids in the water sample.
questions.explanation: Mass of dissolved solids = mass of basin + residue − mass of empty basin = 0.18 g.

questions.question:
A student evaporated a sample of sea water to dryness.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the concentration of dissolved solids in g/dm³.

headers: Volume of sea water in cm³
Mass of solid remaining in g

markScheme: 1 mark: 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³
questions.explanation: Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000, then divide mass by volume.

questions.question:
Tap water contains 0.40 g/dm³ of dissolved solids.
Calculate the mass of solids left when 150 cm³ of tap water is evaporated to dryness.
markScheme: 1 mark: 150 cm³ = 0.150 dm³
questions.explanation: Mass = concentration × volume (in dm³) = 0.40 × 0.150 = 0.060 g.

questions.question:
A student evaporated three 50.0 cm³ portions of a well-water sample.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean concentration of dissolved solids in g/dm³.

headers: Mass of dissolved solids in g

markScheme: 1 mark: 50.0 cm³ = 0.0500 dm³
questions.explanation: Find the mean mass first, then divide by the volume in dm³.

questions.question:
A desalination plant produces 5.0 × 10⁴ m³ of potable water per day.
The plant uses 3.5 kWh of energy per m³ of water.
Calculate the energy used per day.
questions.explanation: Energy = volume × energy per m³ = 50 000 × 3.5 = 175 000 kWh, showing why desalination is so energy intensive.

questions.question: Give two places in the UK where rainwater collects to provide fresh water.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: in the ground (aquifers) / lakes / rivers / reservoirs
questions.explanation: Rain collects underground in porous rock and in surface water such as lakes and rivers.

questions.question: Name two sterilising agents used to treat drinking water.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: chlorine / ozone / ultraviolet light
questions.explanation: All three kill microbes in the water.

questions.question: State why water is sterilised before it is supplied to homes.
markScheme: 1 mark: to kill microbes / bacteria (that could cause disease)
questions.explanation: Sterilising kills harmful microorganisms, making the water safe to drink.

questions.question: Explain why potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense.
markScheme: 1 mark: a pure substance contains only one element or compound
1 mark: potable water contains dissolved salts/ions (and chlorine), so it is a mixture
questions.explanation: In chemistry, pure means a single substance. Tap water is a mixture with low levels of dissolved salts.

questions.question: Describe how a student could find the pH of a water sample.
markScheme: 1 mark: add a few drops of universal indicator (or dip in universal indicator paper)
1 mark: compare the colour with a pH colour chart (or use a calibrated pH meter and read the value)
questions.explanation: A pH meter gives a more precise numerical value than universal indicator.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of producing potable water by desalination.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: can use the large supply of sea water where fresh water is scarce
1 mark: disadvantage: requires large amounts of energy / expensive
questions.explanation: Desalination opens up a huge water source, but the energy cost is very high.

questions.question: A student evaporated 20 cm³ of a water sample and found 0.01 g of dissolved solids. Suggest how the student could improve the method to get a more accurate value for the concentration of dissolved solids.
markScheme: 1 mark: evaporate a larger volume so the mass of solid is larger
1 mark: use a balance with a higher resolution (more decimal places)
1 mark: repeat and calculate a mean / heat to constant mass / heat gently to avoid spitting
questions.explanation: A mass of 0.01 g has a large percentage uncertainty on a 2 decimal place balance. A larger volume and a more precise balance reduce this.

questions.question: State the pH you would expect for pure water.
markScheme: 1 mark: 7

questions.question: Describe how potable water is produced from a river in the United Kingdom.
markScheme: Indicative content: choose an appropriate source of fresh water; screens remove large objects such as twigs; water passes through filter beds of sand and gravel to remove smaller insoluble particles; water is sterilised to kill microbes using chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light; chlorine remains in water to protect it in the pipes.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): filtration and sterilisation described in the correct order with a named sterilising agent and the purpose of each stage.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two stages identified, possibly in the wrong order or without purpose.
questions.explanation: The order is filter then sterilise: solids are removed first so the sterilising agent works on clear water.

questions.question:
A student is given three water samples: tap water, sea water and river water.
Plan an investigation to analyse the samples, by finding the pH and the mass of dissolved solids in each, and then describe how the student could produce a pure sample of water from the sea water.
markScheme: Indicative content: pH: use universal indicator and colour chart or a calibrated pH meter on each sample. Dissolved solids: weigh a clean dry evaporating basin; measure a known volume (for example 25 cm³) with a measuring cylinder or pipette; heat gently over a water bath or Bunsen until dry; allow to cool and reweigh; mass of solid = difference; repeat to constant mass or repeat and take mean; same volume for each sample. Distillation: heat sea water in a flask with a thermometer at the side arm; steam passes into a Liebig condenser (or delivery tube into a test tube in iced water); water condenses and is collected; check thermometer reads 100 °C; test the distillate for no residue or pH 7.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a logical, detailed plan covering pH, dissolved solids with weighing before and after and a fair test, and distillation with how water is collected and shown to be pure.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes at least two parts of the investigation with some detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one part, for example 'boil the water away'.
questions.explanation: Strong answers include measurements (masses, volumes), control variables and a check that the distilled water is pure.

questions.question: Which pair of methods can both be used for desalination?
options: Filtration and chlorination
Distillation and reverse osmosis
Sedimentation and ozone treatment
Chromatography and UV light
markScheme: 1 mark: Distillation and reverse osmosis
questions.explanation: Both remove dissolved salts. The other pairs remove solids or kill microbes but leave salt in the water.

questions.question:
A student evaporated two water samples, X and Y.
Table 1 shows the results.
Which statement is correct?
options: X has the higher concentration of dissolved solids
Both samples have the same concentration
Y has the higher concentration of dissolved solids
The concentrations cannot be compared because the volumes differ
markScheme: 1 mark: Y has the higher concentration
questions.explanation: X: 0.25 ÷ 0.050 = 5.0 g/dm³. Y: 0.15 ÷ 0.025 = 6.0 g/dm³. Converting to concentration allows a fair comparison.
